sections.title: Amoebiasis: the organism, spread and intestinal disease

blocks.text: Amoebiasis is caused by the protozoan **Entamoeba histolytica**. Humans pass it to each other as **cysts**: these are swallowed in water or raw food contaminated by human faeces, and spread can also be direct, including through **oral–anal sexual contact**. It occurs worldwide but is far commoner in the **tropics and subtropics**.

**E. dispar** and **E. moshkovskii** look exactly like E. histolytica down the microscope but are **non-pathogenic**. Telling them apart needs molecular, isoenzyme or monoclonal-antibody methods. Only **E. histolytica** produces amoebic dysentery or a liver abscess.

blocks.title: Pathology in the bowel
items: Swallowed cysts release **trophozoites**, which invade the large-bowel mucosa.
Ulcers are **flask-shaped** (they burrow under the mucosa) and are worst in the **caecum**, though they can reach the anal canal; the mucosa **between ulcers is normal**.
Ulcers may **bleed heavily** but only **rarely perforate**.
**Amoeboma**: an uncommon localised inflammatory granuloma, usually caecal or rectosigmoid. It shows as a rectal mass or a colonic filling defect and can bleed, obstruct or cause intussusception.
Trophozoites can reach the **liver through the portal venous system** and form an abscess (see next section).

blocks.title: Clinical spectrum of intestinal amoebiasis
rows: The **majority** of infections; about **one-third** of people in endemic areas pass cysts without symptoms
Incubation **2 weeks to many years**; offensive diarrhoea **alternating with constipation**, blood or mucus, and **right lower quadrant pain** that can mimic appendicitis
Bloody diarrhoea resembling **bacillary dysentery or ulcerative colitis**; seen especially in **older people**, the **puerperium** and when ulcers are secondarily infected
Risk of **toxic dilatation**, perforation and peritonitis
Stricture after chronic infection, severe haemorrhage, amoeboma, liver abscess

blocks.title: Diagnosing amoebic colitis
items: Examine **fresh stool** or exudate **straight away** for **motile trophozoites that contain ingested red cells**; movement stops as the sample cools.
Sigmoidoscopy may show the flask-shaped ulcers; scrapings should be examined at once.
In chronic disease several stool samples may be needed before cysts are seen.
Serum antibodies are positive in only about **60%** of dysenteric amoebiasis, so a negative test does not exclude colitis.
Differential of bloody diarrhoea: **IBD**, bacillary dysentery, E. coli, Campylobacter, salmonellae and, rarely, pseudomembranous colitis.

blocks.text: **Cysts alone do not prove disease.** The diagnosis of invasive amoebiasis rests on **haematophagous trophozoites** (or tissue invasion). Many "cyst passers" are healthy, and some are carrying the harmless E. dispar.
In a returned traveller with diarrhoea, **fever plus significant blood** in the stool should raise concern for **amoebic dysentery** or an invasive bacterial infection.

blocks.note: Look at panel A: the E. histolytica life cycle, from swallowed cyst to trophozoite, then colonic ulcer, amoeboma and liver abscess.

sections.title: Amoebic liver abscess and treatment of amoebiasis

blocks.text: Trophozoites carried up a **portal venule** multiply in the liver and destroy parenchyma. The abscess is usually **single** and in the **right lobe**. Its fluid starts pinkish and becomes **chocolate-brown ("anchovy sauce")**. It is much commoner in **men (about 9:1)**, and it is a **long-incubation** infection (over 21 days; 8–20 weeks in one source), so it belongs in the differential of fever in a returned traveller.

blocks.title: Clinical picture
items: Often **no diarrhoea** and **no recent dysentery** – do not wait for a bowel history.
**High swinging fever**, sweating and **profound malaise**.
**Tender enlarged liver**, cough and **right shoulder-tip pain** are characteristic.
Right-sided chest signs: **consolidation or effusion**.
Early on symptoms may be vague and signs minimal.

blocks.title: Where an amoebic liver abscess can rupture
rows: Pus coughed up via a **hepatobronchial fistula**
Less common but **more serious**; needs immediate aspiration or surgical drainage
From a **left-lobe** abscess; needs immediate drainage

blocks.title: Investigations for amoebic liver abscess
rows: **Neutrophil leucocytosis**; anaemia, raised ESR, low albumin; **ALP raised, bilirubin often normal**
Confirms the abscess: a rounded **hypoechoic** lesion
Non-enhancing cavity with an enhancing inflammatory rim
Positive in **over 95%** of hepatic amoebiasis (Davidson); ELISA or complement fixation almost always positive
Chocolate-brown pus that **rarely contains free amoebae**

blocks.text: Imaging **cannot reliably separate** an amoebic from a **pyogenic** abscess, and a **hydatid cyst** is the other key differential (check hydatid serology after exposure in the Middle East, Central Asia or parts of Africa). Broad-spectrum antibiotics are often added until a pyogenic cause is excluded.

blocks.title: Drug treatment of amoebiasis (Davidson 24e)
rows: 1. Tissue amoebicide (intestinal and early hepatic disease)
800 mg orally three times daily for 5–10 days
500 mg orally three times daily for 10 days

blocks.title: When to aspirate a liver abscess
items: Most typical abscesses (single, right lobe, traveller or migrant) are **cured by metronidazole without aspiration**.
Aspirate (repeatedly if needed) when the abscess is **large**, **threatens to rupture**, or **responds slowly** to drugs.
Rupture into the **pleura, pericardium or peritoneum** needs **immediate aspiration or surgical drainage**.
A pyogenic abscess, by contrast, is drained percutaneously (often with a pigtail catheter).

blocks.text: **Books disagree on metronidazole doses.** Davidson: 800 mg three times daily for 5–10 days for intestinal and early hepatic disease. Kumar: 800 mg three times daily for 5 days for colitis but **400 mg** three times daily for 5 days for liver abscess. Kumar & Clark Essentials gives 500 mg three times daily for 7–10 days on one page and 800 mg for 10 days on another. **Quote Davidson in the exam.**

**Serology figures differ.** Davidson: immunofluorescence positive in **over 95%** of hepatic amoebiasis and amoeboma but only **about 60%** of dysentery. Kumar and its Essentials: **at least 90%** in liver abscess and **60–70%** in active colitis. Same message either way: strong for the abscess, weak for colitis.
**Always finish with a luminal agent.** Metronidazole treats invading trophozoites, but cysts left in the bowel lumen need **diloxanide furoate** (or paromomycin) to clear them.
Prevention: **boiling** water kills cysts, but **chlorine and iodine** tablets are not always effective. Avoid raw vegetables and unclean water.
Local past papers repeatedly ask for **amoebic liver abscess with its treatment** as an essay and for the drug used in amoebiasis (**metronidazole**) as an MCQ.

blocks.note: Look at panel B: thick chocolate-brown ("anchovy sauce") pus aspirated from an amoebic liver abscess.

blocks.text: **Giardia lamblia** (also called **G. intestinalis**) is a **flagellate** protozoan found worldwide and commonest in developing countries. It is the **parasite most often imported into the UK** and mainly affects **children, travellers and the immunosuppressed**. Mammals, including pets and farm animals, shed cysts in their stool; the cysts stay viable in water for **up to 3 months**, and infection is **faecal–oral**, mostly from **contaminated water**. It also spreads person to person in **day nurseries and residential institutions**, and large water-borne outbreaks have occurred in Europe and rural North America.

blocks.title: How it causes disease
items: The trophozoite **attaches to duodenal and jejunal mucosa** and causes inflammation (a **small-bowel** infection).
Histology usually shows **mild partial villous atrophy**; subtotal atrophy is rare. The damage is probably **immune-mediated**.
Associated **bacterial overgrowth** may add to fat malabsorption.
It is **non-invasive**: watery diarrhoea **without faecal leucocytes**.

blocks.title: Clinical course
rows: Watery diarrhoea, **bloating**, abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea and vomiting; abdomen may be distended and tender
Pale, **bulky, floating, greasy, foul-smelling** stools (**steatorrhoea**), malabsorption and weight loss
Repeated or chronic infection can **stunt growth**

blocks.title: Diagnosis
items: Stool microscopy for **cysts** on samples taken **2–3 days apart** (send three samples for ova and parasites).
**Stool antigen** (ELISA) tests are available.
**Duodenal or jejunal aspirate** at endoscopy gives a **higher yield**; the **string test** samples duodenal fluid after an overnight fast.
**Jejunal biopsy** may show trophozoites on the epithelial surface.
Treatment is often given on **clinical suspicion** alone.

blocks.text: A **negative stool examination does not exclude giardiasis**, because the parasite is shed **intermittently**. Go to duodenal sampling or antigen testing if suspicion stays high.

blocks.title: Treatment of giardiasis
rows: **Tinidazole 2 g single dose**; or metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 10 days; or nitazoxanide 500 mg twice daily for 3 days
Metronidazole **2 g once daily for 3 days** cures most; a second or third course is sometimes needed. Alternatives: tinidazole, nitazoxanide, albendazole (Kumar) or mepacrine (Essentials)

blocks.text: The **metronidazole regimen differs between books**: Davidson gives 400 mg three times daily for 10 days, while Kumar gives 2 g once daily on three successive days. In the exam, give **Davidson's** regimen (or single-dose tinidazole).

Place Giardia correctly in diarrhoea lists: a **watery-diarrhoea** organism (with cholera, rotavirus, ETEC, Cryptosporidium, norovirus), a cause of **chronic diarrhoea** (with IBD and amoebic dysentery), and a **small-bowel malabsorption** cause that must be excluded before diagnosing **tropical sprue**. Protozoa cause **under 5%** of travellers' diarrhoea.

Past-paper favourites: "**Giardiasis – treatment**" as a short essay, and the MCQ "faecal white cells are **absent** in…" with **giardiasis** as the answer (Shigella and enteroinvasive E. coli are invasive).

blocks.note: Look at: Giardia trophozoites lying on the surface of small-intestinal mucosa.

sections.title: Leishmaniasis: the parasite and visceral disease (kala-azar)

blocks.text: **Leishmania** are intracellular **flagellate protozoa** carried by the bite of **female phlebotomine sandflies** (Phlebotomus in the Old World, Lutzomyia in the New World). There are three broad syndromes: **visceral (VL, kala-azar)**, **cutaneous (CL)** and **mucosal (ML)**. Most transmission is **zoonotic** (dog and rodent reservoirs), but in the major **Indian subcontinent VL foci** humans are the **only reservoir**, as they are in injecting drug-users sharing equipment.

blocks.title: Life cycle
items: The sandfly injects **promastigotes** (flagellated, 10–20 μm).
Inside **macrophages** they become **amastigotes** (2–4 μm) = **Leishman–Donovan bodies**, which multiply and burst the cell.
A feeding sandfly takes up amastigotes; in its gut they turn back into promastigotes and migrate to the proboscis.
Sandflies live in cracks of **mud or straw houses** and bite at night.

blocks.note: Look at: promastigote in the sandfly, amastigote in the human macrophage, and which species stay in the dermis, spread to mucosa, or reach the viscera.

blocks.text: VL is caused by the **L. donovani complex** (L. donovani, L. infantum, L. chagasi). **India, Sudan, Bangladesh and Brazil** account for about **90%** of cases. It can also follow blood transfusion and appear in the immunosuppressed (renal transplant, HIV). Most infected people stay asymptomatic; in disease the **spleen, liver, bone marrow and lymph nodes** are involved. Incubation is weeks to months, occasionally years.

blocks.title: Clinical features of visceral leishmaniasis
rows: **High fever with rigors** at onset, then afebrile spells and **relapsing** fever
Enlarges **early** and becomes **massive** (can reach the right iliac fossa)
Common in Africa, the Mediterranean and South America; **rare in India**
**Pancytopenia**: anaemia (can cause cardiac failure); thrombocytopenia with retinal, GI and nasal bleeding
Profound suppression → **secondary infections** (TB, pneumonia, dysentery, skin infections)

blocks.title: Investigations
items: Blood: **pancytopenia** with granulocytopenia and **monocytosis**; **polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia** (mainly IgG); **hypoalbuminaemia**.
**Splenic aspirate** for amastigotes is the most efficient test (**98% sensitive**) but risks **serious bleeding**.
**Bone marrow** or **lymph node** smears are safer but less sensitive; buffy coat smears help in the immunosuppressed; culture and PCR need specialist labs.
Serology: ELISA or immunofluorescence; in endemic areas the **direct agglutination test (DAT)** and **rK39 strip test**. Specific serology is positive in about 95%.
The **leishmanin skin test is usually negative** in active VL, reflecting poor cell-mediated immunity.

blocks.text: **DAT and rK39 stay positive for months after cure**, so they cannot be used to judge response or detect relapse. Formol-gel (aldehyde) and similar globulin tests should **not** be used to diagnose VL.

Differential: **malaria, typhoid, TB, schistosomiasis**. The combination of **fever, splenomegaly, pancytopenia and no response to antimalarials** points to VL. A low platelet count with a big spleen suggests **splenic sequestration**, unlike ITP, which usually has no splenomegaly.

blocks.title: Drug treatment of visceral leishmaniasis
rows: 20 mg/kg/day IV or IM for 28–30 days

Still the mainstay in most regions **except Bihar, India** (about two-thirds refractory). Toxicity: arthralgia, myalgia, raised transaminases, pancreatitis; **cardiotoxicity** – concave ST elevation, **QTc > 0.5 s**, ventricular arrhythmias
India: total 10–15 mg/kg; a **single 10 mg/kg** dose cured 96%
**First line in Europe** and in the Indian subcontinent elimination programme; less toxic
Cure close to 100%; infusion fever and rigors, thrombophlebitis, renal and hepatic toxicity, **hypokalaemia**
Cures over 90%; **teratogenic** – avoid pregnancy during treatment and for **3 months after**
Highly effective; no significant hearing or kidney toxicity reported

blocks.text: **HIV–VL co-infection.** HIV raises the risk of VL **100–1000-fold**. Presentation may be atypical (GI tract, ascites, pleural or pericardial effusion). Parasites are **plentiful**, even in buffy coat, but **serology has low sensitivity**; blood **PCR** is at least 95% sensitive and tracks relapse. Relapse within a year is common, so **monthly liposomal amphotericin B** is used as maintenance.

blocks.title: Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL)
rows: **6 months to 3+ years** after apparent cure
Macules, papules, **nodules** and plaques on the **face (around the chin)**; hypopigmented macules anywhere
Also a **measles-like micropapular rash** over the body
Little spontaneous healing; no systemic upset
Prolonged: Sb for 120 days, repeated amphotericin courses, or miltefosine for 12 weeks

blocks.text: PKDL patients are a **human reservoir**: focal VL outbreaks have been traced to them in previously VL-free areas, which is why they matter for elimination programmes.

blocks.note: Look at: a splenic smear packed with intracellular amastigotes (Leishman–Donovan bodies), with a few lying free.
Compare: Indian PKDL (facial macules, papules, nodules, plaques) with Sudanese PKDL (micronodular rash).

blocks.text: **Cutaneous leishmaniasis** (oriental sore) occurs in the Old World, where it is mild, and in the Americas, where it is a more serious, sometimes disfiguring disease. Incubation is typically **2–3 months**. A **papule at the bite site** slowly grows to **2–10 cm**, and a **crust** forms over an **ulcer with a granular base and raised edge**. Satellite lesions, local lymphadenopathy and secondary infection can occur. Most Old World sores **heal on their own**, leaving a scar.

blocks.title: Old World cutaneous species
rows: **Rapid necrosis, wet sores**; satellite lesions common
Dogs; **urban**, also spread human to human (Afghanistan is the biggest focus)
**Slow, less severe**; can relapse as **leishmaniasis recidivans**
**Solitary facial lesion with satellites**; can become diffuse CL

blocks.title: Other cutaneous patterns
items: **Diffuse CL**: in patients **anergic** to Leishmania (L. aethiopica, L. mexicana, L. amazonensis) the infection spreads from a facial lesion to **non-ulcerating nodules over the whole body**.
**Recidivans (lupoid) leishmaniasis**: L. tropica sores that seem healed keep **relapsing**.
**L. mexicana**: self-healing **chiclero ulcers**; ear-pinna lesions can be chronic and destructive.

blocks.text: **Mucosal leishmaniasis ("espundia")** follows skin infection with **L. (Viannia) braziliensis**, at the same time or **years later**; young men with chronic lesions are most at risk. The **nasal mucosa thickens and reddens from the junction of the nose and upper lip**, then ulcerates; the lips, palate and **larynx** can be destroyed. It **does not heal spontaneously**, and death can follow **respiratory infection**.

Figures for espundia differ: Davidson says **2–40%** of L. braziliensis infections progress to mucosal disease, Kumar says **3–10%**. Follow Davidson. The spelling also varies (**brasiliensis** in Davidson, braziliensis in Kumar).

blocks.title: Diagnosing CL and ML
items: Often clinical, but **confirm the parasite** because other infections mimic it.
**Giemsa-stained slit-skin smear** for amastigotes; culture of the sore (culture of fine-needle aspirate is the most sensitive); **PCR** for species.
ML is harder to confirm: biopsies show scanty organisms.
**Leishmanin skin test**: positive = **> 5 mm induration at 48 h**. It is positive in most CL but **negative in diffuse CL and in active VL**.

blocks.title: Managing CL and ML
items: **Small lesions** may self-heal or are treated with **cryotherapy** (liquid nitrogen) or **curettage**.
Local drugs for CL: topical **paromomycin** or **intralesional antimony**.
**ML**, and CL that is multiple or in a disfiguring site: **parenteral Sb 20 mg/kg/day** (about 20 days for CL, 28 for ML) or **amphotericin B**.
Give Sb to **prevent mucosal disease** if a South American sore could be L. braziliensis.
Kumar names **amphotericin B the treatment of choice for ML** where available; relapses are common.

blocks.title: Prevention and control
items: **Insecticide spraying** and **insecticide-treated nets** (sandflies are tiny).
Where transmission is zoonotic, destroy **infected or stray dogs**.
Where it is anthroponotic, **early diagnosis and treatment** of patients shrinks the reservoir.
Personal protection; sandflies **fly poorly**, so sleeping off the ground helps.
**No vaccine** is available.

blocks.note: Look at: A, the early papule; B, the ulcer with a raised edge and crusted granular base.
Look at: hyperkeratotic nodular lesions and leishmaniasis recidivans on the cheek due to L. tropica.

cards.front: Which Entamoeba species causes dysentery and liver abscess, and how is it told apart from look-alikes?
cards.back: Only **E. histolytica**. E. dispar and E. moshkovskii look identical but are harmless; separate them by molecular, isoenzyme or monoclonal-antibody methods.

cards.front: Shape and usual site of amoebic colonic ulcers?
cards.back: **Flask-shaped** ulcers, worst in the **caecum**, with **normal mucosa** between them.

cards.front: What finding confirms amoebic colitis on stool microscopy?
cards.back: **Motile trophozoites containing ingested red cells** in a fresh, warm sample. Cysts alone do not prove disease.

cards.front: Usual site of an amoebic liver abscess and look of its pus?
cards.back: **Right lobe**, usually single; pus is **chocolate-brown ("anchovy sauce")** and rarely contains free amoebae.
Over **95%** in hepatic amoebiasis and amoeboma; only about **60%** in amoebic dysentery.

cards.front: What must follow metronidazole in amoebiasis, and why?
cards.back: A **luminal amoebicide** – **diloxanide furoate** or paromomycin 500 mg three times daily for 10 days – to clear cysts from the bowel.

cards.front: Indications to aspirate an amoebic liver abscess?
cards.back: **Large**, **threatening to rupture**, or **slow response** to drugs; immediate drainage if it ruptures into pleura, pericardium or peritoneum.

cards.front: Where does Giardia live and what does the biopsy usually show?
cards.back: **Duodenum and jejunum**; usually **mild partial villous atrophy** (subtotal is rare), trophozoites on the surface.
**Tinidazole 2 g single dose** (or metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 10 days, or nitazoxanide).

cards.front: Why does a negative stool test not exclude giardiasis?
cards.back: Cysts are **shed intermittently**; use repeat stools, stool antigen, or **duodenal aspirate**.

cards.front: Most sensitive diagnostic test for visceral leishmaniasis, and its drawback?
cards.back: **Splenic aspirate** for Leishman–Donovan bodies (**98%**); risk of **serious haemorrhage**.

cards.front: Why can rK39 or DAT not be used to follow VL treatment?
cards.back: They stay **positive for months after cure**, so they do not predict response or relapse.
**Concave ST elevation**, **QTc > 0.5 s** and ventricular arrhythmias (milder: T-wave inversion).
**Teratogenic**: no pregnancy during treatment and for **3 months** afterwards.
India: months to years after VL, facial nodules, rarely self-heals. Sudan: ~50% of VL patients, early, micropapular rash, most heal within a year.

cards.front: Which species causes espundia and where does it start?
cards.back: **L. (V.) braziliensis**; starts at the **junction of nose and upper lip**, never heals spontaneously.

cards.front: When is the leishmanin skin test negative?
cards.back: In **diffuse cutaneous** leishmaniasis and **active visceral** leishmaniasis (poor cell-mediated immunity).

questions.stem: A 29-year-old food handler who grew up in an endemic area feels well. Routine stool microscopy reports cysts with the appearance of Entamoeba histolytica. He has no diarrhoea, blood in the stool or abdominal pain.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about this result is correct?
options: The cysts may belong to a harmless look-alike species that only molecular or similar methods can separate
Amoebic serology will be positive in over 95% of people like him
Finding cysts in stool is rare in endemic populations
The cysts must contain ingested red cells to be E. histolytica
questions.explanation: **E. dispar** and **E. moshkovskii** are identical to E. histolytica under the microscope and need molecular, isoenzyme or monoclonal-antibody methods to separate. Cysts alone never prove disease; invasive disease is shown by **haematophagous trophozoites**.
whyNot: Cysts alone do not prove disease; invasion is shown by trophozoites containing red cells.
The >95% figure applies to hepatic amoebiasis and amoeboma; seropositivity is low in asymptomatic cyst passers.
About one-third of people in endemic areas pass cysts without symptoms.
Ingested red cells are a feature of tissue-invading trophozoites, not cysts.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman in Bangladesh, three weeks after delivering her baby, has frequent bloody, mucus-laden stools and lower abdominal pain. A fresh, warm stool sample examined at once shows motile organisms containing ingested red blood cells.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Motile trophozoites with ingested red cells** are diagnostic of invasive E. histolytica. The dysenteric form is seen especially in the **puerperium**, in older people and when ulcers are secondarily infected.
whyNot: Bacillary dysentery can look similar clinically, but the haematophagous amoebae on microscopy settle the diagnosis.
Amoebic dysentery can mimic ulcerative colitis, but UC does not produce motile trophozoites in stool.
Giardia causes non-bloody small-bowel diarrhoea, not dysentery.
Campylobacter is a bacterial cause of bloody diarrhoea; it would not show haematophagous trophozoites.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man returned from India 3 months ago. He has a swinging fever, sweats, right shoulder-tip pain and a tender enlarged liver, but no diarrhoea. Chest X-ray shows a raised right hemidiaphragm and ultrasound shows a single hypoechoic lesion in the right lobe.
questions.leadIn: Which test best supports an amoebic cause?
options: Microscopy of aspirated pus for amoebae
questions.explanation: Antibodies are detectable in **over 95%** of hepatic amoebiasis, and serology is how the diagnosis is usually established. Imaging confirms an abscess but cannot reliably say whether it is amoebic or pyogenic.
whyNot: Many patients have no recent colitis, so stool is often unhelpful, and cysts alone prove nothing.
Aspirated pus is chocolate-brown but only rarely contains free amoebae.
Blood cultures look for a pyogenic abscess; they do not confirm amoebiasis.
The stool antigen test is insensitive for amoebic liver abscess.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has finished 10 days of oral metronidazole for an amoebic liver abscess. His fever has settled and the liver is no longer tender.
questions.leadIn: Which drug should he take next?
questions.explanation: After a tissue amoebicide, a **luminal agent** (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin, 500 mg three times daily for 10 days) clears cysts left in the bowel and prevents relapse and spread.
whyNot: Pentavalent antimony treats leishmaniasis, not amoebiasis.
Liposomal amphotericin B is used for leishmaniasis.
A fluoroquinolone treats invasive bacterial diarrhoea, not luminal amoebic cysts.
Miltefosine is an oral antileishmanial drug.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman developed bloating and watery diarrhoea 2 weeks after drinking stream water on a hiking trip. A month later she passes pale, greasy, floating stools and has lost weight. There is no blood in the stool. Three stool samples for ova and parasites are negative.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most likely to give the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is **giardiasis**: small-bowel diarrhoea becoming steatorrhoea after untreated water. Shedding is intermittent, so negative stools do not exclude it; a **duodenal or jejunal aspirate** gives a higher yield.
whyNot: Sigmoidoscopy looks at the colon; Giardia lives in the duodenum and jejunum.
Amoebic serology is for invasive E. histolytica disease, which causes colitis or liver abscess.
Splenic aspirate is used for visceral leishmaniasis.
Liver ultrasound looks for an abscess and has no role in a small-bowel infection.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old student back from South-East Asia has 3 weeks of bloating and watery diarrhoea. A stool antigen test is positive for Giardia.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, which is a suitable single-dose treatment?
questions.explanation: Davidson lists **tinidazole 2 g as a single dose**, metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 10 days, or nitazoxanide 500 mg twice daily for 3 days.
whyNot: Diloxanide is a luminal amoebicide used after metronidazole in amoebiasis.
Antimony treats leishmaniasis.
A fluoroquinolone treats invasive bacterial diarrhoea; Giardia is a protozoan.
Liposomal amphotericin B is for visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old farm labourer from Bihar has had intermittent fever for 4 months. Two courses of antimalarials have not helped. His spleen reaches the right iliac fossa, his skin has darkened, and he has had nosebleeds. Blood tests show pancytopenia, a low albumin and a high polyclonal globulin level.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia and failure of antimalarials** point to **kala-azar** ("black fever"). Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia and hypoalbuminaemia support it, and the Indian subcontinent is a major focus.
whyNot: Chronic malaria can enlarge the spleen, but repeated antimalarial failure with skin darkening and high globulins fits VL better.
Typhoid is in the differential but does not cause massive splenomegaly with skin darkening over months.
TB is a differential and a common secondary infection in VL, but it does not explain this picture.
Schistosomiasis is a differential, but VL best explains pancytopenia, high globulins and darkened skin.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman in Bihar, India, has confirmed visceral leishmaniasis. She hopes to conceive soon after treatment. The local programme follows current Indian practice.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: **Liposomal amphotericin B** is first line in the Indian elimination programme; a single 10 mg/kg dose cured 96% of Indian patients. Miltefosine is teratogenic, and antimony fails in about two-thirds of cases in Bihar.
whyNot: Miltefosine is teratogenic: pregnancy must be avoided during treatment and for 3 months after.
In Bihar about two-thirds of cases are refractory to antimony.
Pentamidine was abandoned (falling efficacy, diabetes, hypoglycaemia, hypotension).
Metronidazole treats amoebiasis and giardiasis, not leishmaniasis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man from Bolivia had a slow-healing leg ulcer 3 years ago after working in the forest. He now has nasal blockage. The nasal mucosa is thickened and red, starting at the junction of the nose and upper lip, with early ulceration.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Espundia** (mucosal leishmaniasis) follows L. (V.) braziliensis skin infection, sometimes years later, and starts at the **nose–lip junction**. It never heals on its own.
whyNot: L. major is an Old World species causing wet, self-healing skin sores.
L. tropica causes Old World skin sores and recidivans, not mucosal destruction.
L. donovani causes visceral disease (kala-azar).
L. mexicana causes self-healing chiclero ulcers rather than mucosal disease.

questions.stem: A leishmanin skin test (read as induration at 48 hours) is being considered in several patients with Leishmania infection.
questions.leadIn: In which patient is the test expected to be negative?
options: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis with nodules over the whole body
A localised L. major sore on the forearm
A healed L. tropica sore from 2 years ago
An asymptomatic villager in an endemic area
A localised L. mexicana sore on the ear
questions.explanation: The test measures **cell-mediated immunity**. It is positive in most CL and in asymptomatic endemic infection, but **negative in diffuse CL** (anergy) and in **active VL**.
whyNot: Localised CL usually gives a positive test.
The test is positive after resolved infection too; it does not separate active from healed disease.
Positive leishmanin tests are common in asymptomatic endemic infection.
Localised CL usually gives a positive test.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has an amoebic liver abscess 11 cm across, close to the liver capsule. After 5 days of oral metronidazole he is still febrile and the liver is very tender.
questions.leadIn: What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Step 1: most amoebic abscesses settle on metronidazole alone. Step 2: aspiration is needed when the abscess is **large**, **threatens to rupture**, or the **response is slow**. Step 3: this man has all three, so aspirate (repeat if needed) and continue the tissue amoebicide, then give a luminal agent.
whyNot: Diloxanide clears luminal cysts; it does nothing for a large tissue abscess that is not responding.
Antimony treats leishmaniasis.
Serology does not guide treatment here, and stopping would risk rupture.
A fluoroquinolone has no role in amoebic liver abscess.

questions.theme: Choosing the diagnostic test in protozoal infections
questions.leadIn: Pick the most useful investigation in the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Fresh warm stool microscopy for trophozoites

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with advanced HIV has fever, a large spleen and a pleural effusion after living in southern Spain. Leishmania serology is negative. The team wants a sensitive test on blood, avoiding an invasive procedure, that can later be repeated to watch for relapse.
items.explanation: Step 1: fever and splenomegaly in HIV after Mediterranean exposure suggests **VL**. Step 2: serology has **low sensitivity** in HIV co-infection, so a negative result means little. Blood **PCR** is at least 95% sensitive and also tracks relapse. A splenic aspirate is more invasive and carries a bleeding risk.

items.stem: A 30-year-old engineer returns from Peru with a painless ulcer on the forearm. It has a crusted granular base and a raised edge. You want to see the parasite.
items.explanation: Suspected **cutaneous leishmaniasis**: a **Giemsa-stained slit-skin smear** shows amastigotes. Culture and PCR (for species) add to it.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman from Pakistan has a swinging fever, right shoulder-tip pain and tender hepatomegaly. Chest X-ray shows a raised right hemidiaphragm. You need to confirm an abscess.
items.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess is suspected clinically, and **ultrasound confirms** it (a rounded hypoechoic lesion). Serology then supports the amoebic cause.

questions.theme: Protozoal causes of bowel and liver disease
questions.leadIn: Pick the most likely diagnosis in the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy attends a day nursery where several children are unwell. For 6 weeks he has had bloating and pale, foul-smelling stools that float. He is falling off his growth curve. No white cells are seen in the stool.
items.explanation: **Giardiasis**: spread in **day nurseries**, small-bowel malabsorption with **steatorrhoea**, non-invasive (no faecal leucocytes), and chronic infection can **stunt growth**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man who lived in West Africa has a right iliac fossa mass. Barium enema shows a filling defect in the caecum. Amoebic immunofluorescence serology is strongly positive.
items.explanation: Two steps: a caecal mass suggests carcinoma, but **amoeboma** is a granulomatous mass that mimics it, and serology is positive in **over 95%** of amoeboma. It must still be carefully separated from cancer.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man who has sex with men has fever, right upper quadrant pain and nausea. He has had no diarrhoea. Ultrasound shows a single right-lobe lesion and aspiration yields thick chocolate-brown fluid with no organisms seen.
items.explanation: **Amoebic liver abscess**: male predominance (especially MSM), often no bowel history, single right-lobe lesion and "anchovy sauce" pus that rarely contains amoebae.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man from rural Egypt has months of offensive diarrhoea alternating with constipation, mucus and right lower quadrant pain. Sigmoidoscopy shows scattered flask-shaped ulcers with normal mucosa between them.
items.explanation: The chronic alternating bowel habit, RLQ pain and **flask-shaped ulcers separated by normal mucosa** are typical of **amoebic colitis**.

questions.leadIn: Pick the most likely treatment in the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 23-year-old backpacker has bloating and watery diarrhoea. Giardia antigen is found in the stool. She wants a single dose.
items.explanation: Davidson lists **tinidazole 2 g once** for giardiasis.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV has just been cured of visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. His team want to reduce the high chance of relapse in the coming year.
items.explanation: HIV–VL co-infection tends to relapse within a year, so **monthly liposomal amphotericin B** is given as maintenance.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has bloody diarrhoea. Fresh stool shows motile trophozoites containing red cells.
items.explanation: Invasive **amoebic colitis**: a tissue amoebicide (**metronidazole**) then a **luminal amoebicide** (diloxanide furoate) to clear cysts.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man being treated for an amoebic abscess in the left lobe of the liver develops sudden chest pain and breathlessness. Echocardiography shows a new, large pericardial effusion.
items.explanation: Two steps: a **left-lobe** abscess can rupture into the **pericardium**; rupture into the pericardium, pleura or peritoneum needs **immediate aspiration or surgical drainage** as well as drug therapy.

questions.leadIn: Pick the most likely species in the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A soldier based in a desert area where gerbils are common develops several moist, rapidly necrosing skin sores with satellite lesions.
items.explanation: **L. major**: desert-rodent reservoir, **rapid necrosis with wet sores**, satellite lesions common.

items.stem: A farmer from the Ethiopian highlands, where hyraxes live, has a single facial skin lesion surrounded by small satellite lesions.
items.explanation: **L. aethiopica**: hyrax reservoir and **solitary facial lesions with satellites**; in anergic patients it can progress to diffuse CL.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman from Kabul had a slowly evolving, mild skin sore on her cheek that seemed to heal. Since then it has relapsed again and again at the same site.
items.explanation: Urban Old World CL with a **slow, milder** course and **recidivans** relapses is **L. tropica**; Afghanistan is its biggest focus.

items.stem: A villager in the Indian subcontinent develops kala-azar in an area where humans are the only known reservoir and transmission is person to person via sandflies.
items.explanation: Anthroponotic VL in the Indian subcontinent is caused by **L. donovani**.

items.stem: A chicle gatherer in the Mexican forest has a skin ulcer that is expected to heal on its own.
items.explanation: **L. mexicana** causes the self-healing **chiclero ulcers** of Mexico.

questions.leadIn: Pick the drug in the list most likely to be responsible for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man on day 20 of an injectable treatment for visceral leishmaniasis has joint and muscle aches and a raised amylase. His ECG shows concave ST elevation and a QTc of 0.52 s.
items.explanation: Pentavalent **antimony** causes arthralgia, myalgia, pancreatitis and **cardiotoxicity** (concave ST elevation, QTc > 0.5 s, ventricular arrhythmias).

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman is starting an oral 28-day course for visceral leishmaniasis. She is told she must not become pregnant during treatment or for 3 months afterwards.
items.explanation: **Miltefosine** is oral, given for 28 days, and **teratogenic**, with a long half-life, hence the 3-month rule.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man receives an infusion on alternate days at 0.75–1 mg/kg. Each infusion brings fever, rigors and thrombophlebitis, and his potassium is falling while his creatinine rises.
items.explanation: **Conventional (deoxycholate) amphotericin B**: infusion reactions, renal toxicity and **hypokalaemia**. Lipid formulations are less toxic.

items.stem: An older drug once used for antimony-refractory visceral leishmaniasis was dropped after patients developed hypoglycaemia, later insulin-dependent diabetes, and hypotension.
items.explanation: **Pentamidine** was abandoned for VL because of falling efficacy and **type 1 diabetes, hypoglycaemia and hypotension**.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 60 cells/mm³ has fever, a large spleen and a pleural effusion. Visceral leishmaniasis is suspected.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about his likely co-infection is correct?
options: Leishmania serology may well be negative
Parasites will be scanty and hard to find
Relapse after successful treatment is rare
HIV does not change the risk of acquiring visceral leishmaniasis
The clinical picture is always the classic triad alone
questions.explanation: In HIV–VL co-infection **serology has low sensitivity**, while parasites are **plentiful** (even in buffy coat) and blood PCR is at least 95% sensitive. Atypical sites such as effusions and the GI tract are seen.
whyNot: Parasites are numerous and easily seen, even in buffy coat preparations.
Relapse within a year is common, hence monthly maintenance liposomal amphotericin B.
HIV increases the risk of VL 100–1000-fold.
Low CD4 counts bring atypical presentations, such as effusions and GI involvement.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl in a day nursery has 2 weeks of watery diarrhoea and bloating with no blood. Stool microscopy shows no white cells.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Giardia** is a **non-invasive** small-bowel parasite that causes watery diarrhoea without faecal leucocytes, and it spreads in day nurseries.
whyNot: Shigella invades the colonic mucosa and causes bloody, inflammatory diarrhoea.
Enteroinvasive E. coli invades the mucosa, so faecal white cells are expected.
E. histolytica invades the colon, causing bloody stools.
Campylobacter is a cause of bloody diarrhoea.

questions.theme: Long-incubation protozoal illness in travellers and migrants
questions.leadIn: Pick the most likely diagnosis in the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 9-year-old Sudanese boy was treated for kala-azar 2 months ago. He now has a measles-like rash of tiny papules all over his body, with no fever.
items.explanation: Sudanese **PKDL** appears during VL or within 6 months, affects about half of patients, may show a **micropapular rash**, and often heals on its own.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man drank untreated water while trekking in South Asia. Ten weeks after returning he has fever, cough, right shoulder pain and a tender liver. ALP is raised but bilirubin is normal.
items.explanation: A long-incubation illness after **unpurified water**, with fever, right shoulder pain and **tender hepatomegaly**: **amoebic liver abscess**. ALP raised with normal bilirubin is typical.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man from Nepal has had relapsing fever for months despite antimalarials. His spleen is enormous, his skin has darkened, and he has pancytopenia with nosebleeds.
items.explanation: Two steps: failure of antimalarials argues against malaria; **massive spleen, pancytopenia, bleeding and skin darkening** fit **kala-azar**.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man from Peru has progressive destruction of the nasal septum and soft palate several years after a healed leg ulcer. Biopsy PCR confirms Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Mucosal leishmaniasis needs **systemic** therapy: parenteral antimony or **amphotericin B** (Davidson), and Kumar calls amphotericin the treatment of choice where available. Relapses are common.
whyNot: Cryotherapy is for small cutaneous lesions, not mucosal disease.
Topical paromomycin is used for cutaneous, not mucosal, leishmaniasis.
Mucosal leishmaniasis never heals spontaneously and can be fatal.
Metronidazole has no antileishmanial role.

questions.theme: Interpreting test results in protozoal infection
questions.leadIn: Pick the interpretation in the list that best fits each patient below. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman finished treatment for kala-azar 4 months ago. She is afebrile and gaining weight, her spleen is smaller and her blood counts have recovered. A repeat rK39 strip test is still positive.
items.explanation: Clinical recovery (fever gone, smaller spleen, weight gain, normal counts) means **cure**; **rK39 stays positive for months** and cannot detect relapse.

items.stem: A 37-year-old Ethiopian man has non-ulcerating nodules spreading over his face, trunk and limbs from an old facial lesion. His leishmanin skin test is negative.
items.explanation: Widespread **non-ulcerating nodules** in an **anergic** patient (negative leishmanin test), linked to L. aethiopica, is **diffuse CL**.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student from an endemic area has no symptoms. A stool sample shows Entamoeba cysts but no trophozoites, and amoebic serology is negative.
items.explanation: Cysts without trophozoites, no symptoms and negative serology: **asymptomatic cyst passage** (possibly E. dispar). Cysts alone do not mean disease.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has dysentery due to proven E. histolytica. His doctor sends amoebic immunofluorescence serology.
questions.leadIn: Roughly what proportion of patients with amoebic dysentery have positive serology (Davidson)?
questions.explanation: Davidson: antibodies in **over 95%** of hepatic amoebiasis and amoeboma, but only **about 60%** of dysenteric amoebiasis. Kumar gives 60–70% for active colitis. A negative test does not rule out colitis.
whyNot: Over 95% is the figure for hepatic amoebiasis and amoeboma, not dysentery.
98% is the sensitivity of splenic aspirate in visceral leishmaniasis.
About one-third is the proportion of symptomless cyst passers in endemic areas, not a serology figure.
Serology is far more sensitive than this, even in colitis.

ospe.identify: Splenic aspirate with many **Leishman–Donovan bodies** (amastigotes) inside macrophages → **visceral leishmaniasis**; splenic smear is the most sensitive test (98%).
**Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis**: Indian type with facial macules, papules, nodules and plaques; Sudanese type with a micronodular rash.
**Cutaneous leishmaniasis**: an early papule at the bite site, then an ulcer with a raised edge and crusted granular base.
Hyperkeratotic nodular **cutaneous leishmaniasis** with **leishmaniasis recidivans** on the cheek → **L. tropica**.
Thick **chocolate-brown ("anchovy sauce")** aspirate → **amoebic liver abscess**; free amoebae are rarely seen in it.
**Giardia** trophozoites on the surface of small-intestinal mucosa → **giardiasis** (duodenum and jejunum).
